title: Fixed-Point Reasoners: Stable and Adaptive Deep Looped Transformers
claim: Our method reaches higher accuracy with less compute than the baseline at every difficulty level, with the largest gain on the hardest tasks.
layout: 1 panel, accuracy vs log-compute curves, difficulty color bar on top, callout annotation
description: A single line plot with test accuracy (%) on the y-axis and inference compute in effective layers on a log x-axis from about 2 to 10^4. A color bar above the plot labels task difficulty: light blue for easy, purple for medium, red for hard. Each difficulty gets two curves. Solid lines with filled circles are FPRM (ours), and dashed lines with hollow squares are the TRM baseline. The markers show where each halting rule stops. The solid curves rise earlier and sit above the dashed ones. On easy tasks both curves reach 100%, but FPRM halts earlier. On hard tasks FPRM plateaus near 75% while TRM is near 68%. A dotted circle with an arrow points to a red callout reading '+10 accuracy points ~1k (27%) layers less compute'. A legend sits at the bottom right.
caption: Signal propagation and adaptivity, FPRM vs. TRM: Sudoku-Extreme performance as a function of compute across difficulty levels. Despite being non-hierarchical, FPRM scales better, and identifies accuracy plateaus more effectively by using fixed-point halting.
abstract: Looped architectures provide an inductive bias toward learning step-by-step procedures for tasks that require compositional reasoning. Increasing the effective layers of looped architectures can improve their reasoning capabilities. Similar to deep architectures, looped architectures are prone to a signal propagation problem induced by depth as the halting decision is postponed. In this paper, we address the signal propagation issue by using pre-norm layers and residual scaling. By improving signal propagation, we achieve competitive performance without hierarchical looping, resulting in a simpler architecture than previous state-of-the-art models evaluated on puzzle reasoning tasks. Building on these modifications, we propose FPRM: a Transformer-based Fixed-Point Reasoning Model that uses fixed-point convergence as an end-to-end halting mechanism in a looped architecture. We show that fixed-point halting allows FPRM to adapt its compute to the difficulty of the task. FPRM proves effective on common reasoning benchmarks, namely sudoku, maze, state-tracking and ARC-AGI.
